raw_case_text:
A 37-year-old Japanese man presented to our hospital with a nonproductive cough of two weeks in duration. He did not have fever or dyspnea. He had a history of right hemiparesis, intellectual disability with pica, and symptomatic epilepsy caused by intracerebral hemorrhage, which occurred at two years of age. He had never smoked or consumed alcoholic beverages.
His initial vital signs were as follows: blood pressure, 105/55 mm Hg; pulse rate, 70 beats/minute; respiratory rate, 18 breaths/min; SpO2, 93% in room air; body temperature, 36.5 C. There was no lymphadenopathy. Auscultation revealed no chest rales. A cardiovascular examination was normal, and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops were detected. Abdominal and neurological examinations were unremarkable, and the patient had no rash or petechiae. A chest radiograph revealed bilateral diffuse infiltration (Figure 1). Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed bilateral airspace consolidation and ground-glass opacity (Figure 2).
The patient's laboratory test values were as follows: hemoglobin, 14.9 g/dl; white blood cell count, 8,850/mm3 with a left shift; platelets, 329,000/mm3; serum aspartate aminotransferase 29 U/L (normal, 0-35 U/l); serum alanine aminotransferase, 31 U/L (normal, 0-35 U/l); serum lactate dehydrogenase, 425 U/L (normal, 119-229 U/l); serum total protein, 5.3 g/dl (normal, 6.5-8 g/dl); serum albumin, 2.1 g/dl (normal, 4-5 g/dl); serum C-reactive protein, 9.18 mg/dl (normal, < 0.2 mg/dl); serum KL-6, 2940 U/ml (normal, < 500 U/ml); serum surfactant protein D, 173.0 ng/ml (normal, < 109.9 ng/mL); and serum surfactant protein A, 115.0 ng/ml (normal, < 43.8 ng/mL). The patient's serum was negative for rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibodies. The serum levels of immunoglobulin M, G, and A were within the normal ranges. An electrocardiogram revealed normal findings. An examination of the patient's sputum showed no predominant pathogen and no acid-fast organisms were observed on staining. Two sets of blood cultures were prepared at the time of admission; however, they did not yield any organisms.
The patient underwent a fiberoptic bronchoscopic examination that revealed a normal endobronchial system, and combined bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL)/transbronchial biopsy (TBLB) was performed. BAL fluid (BALF) was obtained from the right middle lobe. The results of the BALF analysis were as follows: histiocytes, 87%; neutrophils, 6%; lymphocytes, 4%; and eosinophils, 3%. Routine cultures of bronchial the washings were negative. The TBLB sample from the right upper lobe revealed alveolar septal thickening due to chronic inflammation, as well as collagen-type fibrosis.
After these examinations, the patient was diagnosed with acute interstitial pneumonia, and intravenous levofloxacin (500 mg) was administered once daily with corticosteroid pulse therapy (methylprednisolone [1000 mg] for three days) followed by prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day). On the 5th day after the initiation of therapy, his respiratory condition worsened and noninvasive positive pressure ventilation was started. His interstitial pneumonia was thought to be getting worse, and cyclophosphamide (500 mg/body) was administered intravenously. On the same day, an additional examination revealed the elevation of the serum (1-3) beta-D glucan (BG) level (104.3 pg/ml; normal, <6.0 pg/ml). He was therefore suspected to have fungal infection or PCP, and voriconazole (200 mg, every 12 hours) and sulfamethoxazole trimethoprim (1600 mg and 320 mg, respectively, every 8 hours) were started. An additional HIV antibody test was negative and the serum protein electrophoresis revealed normal findings. Despite the additional antifungal therapy, his respiratory status gradually worsened, and intravenous corticosteroid pulse therapy (methylprednisolone [1000 mg] for three days) and cyclophosphamide therapy (500 mg/body) were each administered a second time, on the 8th and 11th days, respectively, without improvement. The patient died due to respiratory failure on the 12th day.
A postmortem pathological examination of the lung tissue demonstrated that the alveolar spaces were filled with foamy amorphous material composed of abundant numbers of cystic forms of Pneumocystis jirovecii and cellular debris, as well as an inflammatory reaction with hyaline membranes (Figure 3). Retrospectively, Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) staining of the BALF and TBLB samples obtained on the day of admission revealed a small amount of the cystic form of Pneumocystis jirovecii (Figure 4). It was therefore thought that PCP had been present on the day of his admission.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 37-year-old Japanese man with intellectual disability, right hemiparesis, and epilepsy presented with a 2-week history of nonproductive cough without fever or dyspnea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the hospital with a 2-week history of isolated dry cough without fever or shortness of breath.
subjective.past_medical_history: Right hemiparesis, intellectual disability with pica, and symptomatic epilepsy secondary to an intracerebral hemorrhage at 2 years of age. Lifetime nonsmoker and non-drinker.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for a 2-week nonproductive cough; negative for fever, dyspnea, rash, or petechiae on presentation.

objective.physical_examination: Initial vital signs: Blood pressure 105/55 mmHg, pulse 70 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, SpO2 93% on room air, and body temperature 36.5 °C. Physical examination: No palpable lymphadenopathy; clear lung auscultation without rales; normal cardiac, abdominal, skin, and baseline neurological examinations.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: Hemoglobin 14.9 g/dL, WBC 8,850/mm3 with left shift, platelets 329,000/mm3, AST 29 U/L (normal: 0–35 U/L), ALT 31 U/L (0–35 U/L), elevated LDH 425 U/L (119–229 U/L), hypoproteinemia 5.3 g/dL (6.5–8.0 g/dL), hypoalbuminemia 2.1 g/dL (4.0–5.0 g/dL), and elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) 9.18 mg/dL (<0.2 mg/dL). Interstitial lung biomarkers: Markedly elevated serum KL-6 at 2,940 U/mL (<500 U/mL), surfactant protein D (SP-D) 173.0 ng/mL (<109.9 ng/mL), and surfactant protein A (SP-A) 115.0 ng/mL (<43.8 ng/mL). Immunological and microbiological screening: HIV antibody negative; RF and ANA negative; normal serum IgG, IgA, IgM, and serum protein electrophoresis; negative sputum AFB stain and routine culture; two sets of blood cultures negative. Electrocardiogram: Normal. Chest radiograph: Bilateral diffuse pulmonary infiltration.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT scan: Bilateral airspace consolidation and diffuse ground-glass opacities. Admission fiberoptic bronchoscopy with right middle lobe bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and right upper lobe transbronchial lung biopsy (TBLB): Normal endobronchial tree; BALF differential showed 87% histiocytes, 6% neutrophils, 4% lymphocytes, and 3% eosinophils with negative routine bacterial cultures; initial TBLB H&E reading noted chronic inflammatory alveolar septal thickening and collagen fibrosis. Day 5 fungal biomarker: Elevated serum (1,3)-beta-D-glucan at 104.3 pg/mL (normal <6.0 pg/mL). Post-mortem lung autopsy and retrospective Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) staining of admission BALF/TBLB: Autopsy revealed alveolar spaces filled with foamy amorphous exudate containing abundant Pneumocystis jirovecii cysts, cellular debris, and hyaline membranes; retrospective GMS staining of the admission BALF and TBLB confirmed Pneumocystis jirovecii cysts had been present on admission.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Fatal HIV-negative Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) in a 37-year-old man without traditional pharmacologic immunosuppression, definitively confirmed by post-mortem lung histopathology, retrospective Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) staining of admission BALF and transbronchial lung biopsy specimens, and elevated day 5 serum (1,3)-beta-D-glucan (104.3 pg/mL), after being initially misdiagnosed as acute interstitial pneumonia. Plan and clinical course: Initially treated for presumed acute interstitial pneumonia with IV levofloxacin (500 mg daily) and pulse methylprednisolone (1,000 mg/day for 3 days) followed by prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day). On hospital day 5, respiratory deterioration prompted noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation, IV cyclophosphamide (500 mg), and—upon receipt of the elevated beta-D-glucan result—oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (320 mg/1,600 mg q8h) plus voriconazole (200 mg q12h). Despite repeat steroid pulse (day 8) and cyclophosphamide (day 11), the patient died of refractory respiratory failure on hospital day 12.
